reference: A. Loop diuretics Examples: Furosamide, bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid. Leads to excretion of 20 to 25% of the filtered Na+ when given in maximum dosage. Act on the medullary and cortical aspects of the thick ascending limb, including the macula densa cells in the early distal tubule. At each of these sites Na+ entry is primarily mediated by a Na+ K+ 2Cl- carrier in the luminal membrane that is activated when all 4 sites are occupied. The loop diuretics appear to compete for the Cl- site on this carrier, thereby diminishing net reabsorption. Also, inhibiting the reabsorption of NaCl leads to a parallel reduction in the reabsorption of Ca2+ thereby enhancing Ca2+ excretion. B. Thiazide-Type Diuretics They primarily inhibit sodium and chloride transport in the distal tubule, the connecting segment at the end of the distal tubule, and possibly the early cortical collecting tubule. Since these segments reabsorb less of the filtered load, these diuretics are less potent, inhibiting at most 3 to 5 percent of the filtered Na+. The thiazides inhibit NaCl reabsorption in these segments by competing for the Cl- site on the Na-Cl cotransporter. Another important action is the increased reabsorption of Ca2+ in the distal tubule and cortical collecting tubule. The fall in Ca2+ excretion is useful in the treatment of recurrent kidney stones due to hypocalciuria. C. Potassium-Sparing Diuretics 3 major ones: Amiloride, spironolactone and triamferenc. They act in the principal cells in the cortical collecting tubule (and possibly in the papillary or inner medullary collecting duct). These drugs act by decreasing the number of open Na+ channels. Spironolactone does this indirectly by competitively inhibiting the effect of aldosterone. D. Mannitol This is a nonreabsorbable polysaccharide that acts as an osmotic diuretic. Its main mechanism of action is by inhibiting Na+ and water reabsorption in the proximal tubule and more importantly, in the loop of Henle. It produces a relative water diuresis in which water is lost in excess of Na+ and K+. It can increase plasma osmolality by 2 mechanisms a) The preferential water diuresis following repeated administration can lead to a water deficit and hypernatraemia. b) Hypertonic mannitol may be retained in patients with renal failure, directly increasing the plasma osmolality. In this setting, water movement out of cells down an osmotic gradient will lower the plasma Na+ concentration by dilution. This is an important condition to recognise, since treatment must be aimed at the hyperosmolality, not the hyponatraemia.
